bibl.title: Stimulus-specific regulation of visual oddball differentiation in posterior parietal cortex

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how single neurons in a higher-order visual area distinguish a frequently presented stimulus from a rare one, and whether that depends on which stimulus the local population prefers
span.quote: To address this gap in knowledge, we recorded PPC activity using 2-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology during a visual oddball paradigm. Calcium imaging results reveal differentiation at the level of single neurons for frequent versus rare conditions which varied depending on whether the stimulus was preferred or non-preferred by the recorded neural population. Such differentiation of oddball conditions was mediated primarily by stimulus-independent adaptation in the frequent condition.

span.label: whether the mismatch response is driven by adaptation to the standard or by an enhanced response to the deviant, and whether it depends on stimulus tuning
span.quote: However, whether the MMN is dominated by adaptation to the standard condition or an enhanced response to the deviant condition remains a matter of debate

span.label: the mismatch response appears only for the population-preferred stimulus and is carried almost entirely by adaptation to the standard rather than by surprise at the deviant
span.quote: To address this gap in knowledge, we recorded PPC activity using 2-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology during a visual oddball paradigm. Calcium imaging results reveal differentiation at the level of single neurons for frequent versus rare conditions which varied depending on whether the stimulus was preferred or non-preferred by the recorded neural population. Such differentiation of oddball conditions was mediated primarily by stimulus-independent adaptation in the frequent condition.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Such differentiation of oddball conditions was mediated primarily by stimulus-independent adaptation in the frequent condition.

span.label: visual mismatch negativity in the oddball paradigm
span.quote: The oddball paradigm is a classic sensory stimulus assay used to evaluate neural differentiation of stimulus presentation frequency 1 , 2 .

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To address this gap in knowledge, we recorded PPC activity using 2-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology during a visual oddball paradigm.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Neurons tuned to the presented stimulus adapt strongly while it is the frequent standard but keep their response high when it is the rare deviant, and this asymmetry is what separates the two conditions.
span.quote: To differentiate the deviant and standard conditions, the local neurons that prefer the presented stimulus show substantial adaptation in the standard condition while activity during the deviant condition remains high; whereas the opponent stimulus does not show oddball condition discrimination in the neural activity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Activity is actively suppressed in the opponent stimulus' deviant condition, which is what makes the mismatch response stimulus-specific and could amplify signal relative to noise.
span.quote: We believe the stimulus-specific component of the MMR could arise from suppression of activity in the opponent stimulus’ deviant condition.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the two opposing-direction gratings share one orientation, and orientation does not change between standard and deviant, orientation-dominated responses to the opponent stimulus carry no condition difference.
span.quote: Since orientation remains invariant across standard and deviant conditions, this may explain the lack of MMN for the opponent stimulus.

span.label: the mismatch response decomposes into deviance detection, deviant against control, and stimulus-specific adaptation, control against standard
span.quote: The MMR can be dissected into two key components characterizing the surprise (deviance detection—DD) and adaptation (stimulus-specific adaptation—SSA) responses by comparing the control condition to the deviant or standard condition, respectively. To investigate the distribution of condition-dependent responses across ROIs, we reanalyzed the data by computing condition contrasts (ie. MMR, DD, and SSA) as a function of stimuli for each ROI

span.label: adaptation is present for both stimuli and to a similar degree, so it cannot be what makes the mismatch response stimulus-specific
span.quote: In the distribution of time-averaged SSA across ROIs, both stimuli showed a similar amount of adaptation (Fig. 4 H; preferred stimulus: μ = 2.067, σ = 1.490; opponent stimulus: μ = 1.555, σ = 1.018; stimulus contrast: μ = -0.512, σ = 1.616; paired t test; t (72) = 0.659, p = 0.512; Holm-Bonferroni corrected).

span.label: the specificity is proposed to come instead from suppression of the opponent stimulus in its deviant condition, which would amplify the contrast between conditions
span.quote: Finally, it is important to reconcile that we observed stimulus-specific MMR in the calcium imaging results, but SSA for both stimuli. We believe the stimulus-specific component of the MMR could arise from suppression of activity in the opponent stimulus’ deviant condition. Such a phenomenon could serve as a signal-to-noise amplification mechanism for stimulus presentation frequency differentiation in the local PPC circuitry.

span.label: the MMN can be explained primarily by adaptation, with single-cell calcium imaging revealing putative neurons that showed more prominent MMN and adaptation for one stimulus over the other
span.quote: An important visual oddball study in monkey inferior temporal (IT) cortex revealed stronger responses in the deviant condition compared to the standard (MMN), but failed to find a difference between deviant and many-standard equiprobable control condition 14 . Here we find similar results where the MMN can be explained primarily by adaptation; however, our single-cell 2-photon calcium imaging analysis revealed putative neurons that showed more prominent MMN and adaptation for one stimulus over the other.

span.label: somatostatin interneurons are raised as the circuit element, since inactivating them impairs frequency differentiation in population activity
span.quote: Alternatively, recent work has provided support for the causal involvement of somatostatin-positive (SOM+) neurons in MMN modulation 54 . Inspired by reports of inhibitory interneuron involvement in lateral inhibition and regulation of surround suppression 56 , 57 , one mechanistic explanation could be that these SOM+ neurons facilitating SSA by inhibiting pyramidal neurons during the standard condition 36 . Indeed, evidence shows that the suppression of activity may arise from SOM+ interneurons regulation of pyramidal neurons, as reversible inactivation of SOM+ neurons impair differentiation of stimulus presentation frequency in population activity

span.label: the opponent stimulus shares its orientation with the preferred one, and orientation does not change between conditions, which could by itself explain the missing effect
span.quote: Finally, it is possible to explain the stimulus-specific MMN results in the context of the multiplexing of stimulus direction and orientation. Stimuli with opposing directions share the same orientation and therefore with the stimuli chosen in our study, PPC neurons may contend with both orientation and direction information. This is particularly important for the opponent stimulus where PPC activity could be dominated more by the stimulus orientation rather than direction. Since orientation remains invariant across standard and deviant conditions, this may explain the lack of MMN for the opponent stimulus.

span.label: Without a behavioural readout the study cannot measure stimulus salience for the animal.
span.quote: The caveat of our study is that we can not truly measure saliency of the stimulus and condition to the animal without a behavioral measure; future studies would benefit from including an additional trial condition that requires the animal to make a response to rare or frequently-presented stimuli.

span.label: Using only drifting stimuli means the effect of orientation tuning on oddball differentiation could not be examined.
span.quote: Since we focused on drifting stimuli that PPC was reported to respond strongly to, we are not able to examine how orientation tuning affects oddball condition differentiation.

span.label: GCaMP6f's low signal-to-noise ratio may have hidden additional responsive neurons.
span.quote: It is also possible that using the GCaMP6f calcium indicator reduced our ability to resolve additional responsive neurons due to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR); future studies could benefit from GCaMP6s which possesses superior fluorescence SNR.

span.label: The proposed topographic model of PPC oddball processing is not yet substantiated.
span.quote: We recognize that follow-up work is required to substantiate this theory; particularly an exhaustive testing of static orientations and all motion directions in each permutation of standard, deviant, and control conditions across a larger area of PPC is required.

span.label: The long interval between virus injection and recording may have caused GCaMP6f overexpression.
span.quote: It is possible that such a period of time between virus injection and data acquisition may result in overexpression of GCaMP6f; however upon inspection of mean fluorescence images (Supplementary Fig. 1 ), we found at most 2–3 cells out of each animal’s FOV to exhibit nuclear filling.

span.label: the visual cortex comparison cannot be interpreted because the oddball stimuli were selected by parietal preference
span.quote: MMN was not found to be significant for either stimuli in the VC ERPs (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). Although the difference between standard and deviant responses for Stimulus A is trending (t(6) = 2.36, p = 0.056), these results are difficult to interpret since the oddball stimuli were chosen based on PPC preference.

span.label: saliency to the animal cannot be measured at all without a behavioural response, which this design does not have
span.quote: The caveat of our study is that we can not truly measure saliency of the stimulus and condition to the animal without a behavioral measure; future studies would benefit from including an additional trial condition that requires the animal to make a response to rare or frequently-presented stimuli.

span.label: only drifting stimuli were used, so the effect of orientation tuning on oddball differentiation could not be examined
span.quote: The experimental paradigm used in this study was based on recent visual oddball studies for consistency and was used to accommodate previous reports of motion direction tuning in PPC 22 , 23 ; however, we acknowledge limits in the insight that can be gained given this design. For example, our PPC tuning curves indicate strong orientation tuning. Since we focused on drifting stimuli that PPC was reported to respond strongly to, we are not able to examine how orientation tuning affects oddball condition differentiation.

span.label: the indicator's signal-to-noise ratio may have limited how many responsive neurons could be resolved
span.quote: It is also possible that using the GCaMP6f calcium indicator reduced our ability to resolve additional responsive neurons due to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR); future studies could benefit from GCaMP6s which possesses superior fluorescence SNR.

span.label: the interval between injection and recording could have caused overexpression, checked by counting nuclear-filled cells
span.quote: It is possible that such a period of time between virus injection and data acquisition may result in overexpression of GCaMP6f; however upon inspection of mean fluorescence images (Supplementary Fig. 1 ), we found at most 2

span.label: tuning was only roughly stable across sessions, with the non-preferred response growing, and the possible plasticity was not tested
span.quote: PPC tuning was roughly maintained across sessions (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). The magnitude of the non-preferred stimulus increased over the sessions. This could be explained by plasticity of PPC tuning over the course of repeated presentation of stimuli; however testing this hypothesis was outside the scope of the current study.

span.label: the two modalities were recorded in separate groups of animals
span.quote: With this finding that PPC electrophysiological signatures exhibit MMR as a function of stimulus preference, we next aimed to understand the single neuron basis of this phenomenon by using 2-photon calcium imaging in a separate group of animals

span.label: the mismatch negativity and its 150 to 250 ms window, imported whole into an animal preparation
span.quote: Specifically, the mismatch negativity (MMN) is a neurophysiological difference waveform peaking in the 150–250 ms window after stimulus onset. The MMN refers to the difference in evoked response to the standard and deviant stimulus. Importantly, the MMN is distinct from the N100 (occurring between 50 and 150 ms post stimulus onset) and the P300 (occurring around 300–400 ms) components with respect to function and timing relative to stimulus onset

span.label: the many-standards control block, which is what makes the adaptation and surprise components separable
span.quote: A third block’s (many-standards control block) stimuli consisted of 10 equiprobable drifting gratings of different motion directions (same structure and stimuli as the initial tuning curve session); stimuli presented in this third condition served as controls that do not elicit adaptation effects of the standard condition or surprise effects like the deviant condition.

span.label: ROIs kept only where stimulus-evoked activity ran 1.5 standard deviations above baseline for at least 400 consecutive milliseconds on at least 25% of trials, and in the trial average
span.quote: ROIs that exhibited stimulus-evoked activity (300–1,500 ms) 1.5 standard deviations above baseline (− 200 to 0 ms) mean activity for at least 400 consecutive milliseconds for at least 25% of trials, and 1.5 standard deviations above baseline mean activity for at least 400 consecutive milliseconds in the trial average were identified as visually responsive and were included for further analysis (n = 73).

span.label: the mismatch negativity as a biomarker of sensory processing deficits, which is the stated reason for wanting a cellular account
span.quote: Our results may provide insight to the mechanisms underlying the dysfunction of oddball-related sensory processing deficits in psychiatric disorders. One prominent mechanistic theory in schizophrenia research revolves around the role of N-methyl D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr)-dependent parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneuron activity 37 – 39 . Gamma oscillations arise from the interaction between excitatory pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons 40 – 42 . Further, NMDArs are causally involved in the regulation of PV+ neuron-mediated gamma oscillations 43 . As reduced gamma power has been associated with cognitive and sensory processing deficits in patients with schizophrenia 39 , 44 , it is hypothesized that NMDAr and PV+ interneuron dysfunction are underlying causes

span.label: BOTH oddball blocks run - A as deviant with B standard, then the assignment switched - so every stimulus appears in both roles
span.quote: The reason for presenting both of these blocks is to be able to compare the same stimulus presented in different conditions, thus removing the confounding factor of stimulus-preference when examining neural activity.

span.label: a third MANY-STANDARDS block of ten equiprobable drifting gratings, each direction as rare as the deviant but none of them surprising
span.quote: stimuli presented in this third condition served as controls that do not elicit adaptation effects of the standard condition or surprise effects like the deviant condition

span.label: random salt-and-pepper white-noise images presented BETWEEN the oddball blocks
span.quote: were presented in between the oddball paradigm blocks to reset the visual system and minimize adaptation

span.label: THE SAME CONTRAST GETS A DIFFERENT NAME UNDER A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT: deviant minus standard is called mismatch negativity in the electrophysiology and mismatch response in the calcium imaging, because the indicator's responses go up rather than down and decay slowly
span.quote: The comparison between standard and deviant conditions for the calcium imaging data was called mismatch response (MMR) due to the GCaMP protein exhibiting primarily positive increases in activity and its slow decay kinetics.

span.label: and the analysis window is set by the indicator rather than by the phenomenon - 300 to 1,500 ms is chosen because that is when the calcium signal has decayed, not because that is when the process happens
span.quote: Due to the slow decay kinetics of the GCaMP6f fluorescence indicator, it is difficult to interpret when certain processes are occurring during periods of neural activity. Accordingly, we chose the period of time that calcium responses largely decayed back to baseline (from 300 to 1,500 ms relative to stimulus onset) when performing statistics or averaging across the epoch of time related to stimulus response.

span.label: A THIRD CONDITION IS BUILT TO CONTAIN NEITHER RIVAL: the many-standards block is rare like the deviant and unrepeated like nothing else, so it elicits neither adaptation nor surprise and lets the difference be split in two
span.quote: A third block’s (many-standards control block) stimuli consisted of 10 equiprobable drifting gratings of different motion directions (same structure and stimuli as the initial tuning curve session); stimuli presented in this third condition served as controls that do not elicit adaptation effects of the standard condition or surprise effects like the deviant condition.

span.label: and the same two stimuli swap roles between blocks, which removes stimulus preference as a confound by construction rather than by correction
span.quote: In one block (oddball A), the two best responsive stimuli from the first session were chosen to be presented in either the standard (90% of trials) or deviant (10% of trials) condition (ie. stimulus A was the deviant and B was the standard). In another block (oddball B), the same two stimuli were used but the conditions were switched (ie. stimulus B was the deviant and A was the standard). The reason for presenting both of these blocks is to be able to compare the same stimulus presented in different conditions, thus removing the confounding factor of stimulus-preference when examining neural activity.

span.label: THE NULL IS CONSTRUCTED FROM WHAT THE ARTEFACT CANNOT DO: shuffling trial labels within a block preserves every block-to-block difference and destroys only the condition difference, and that shuffle is subtracted region by region
span.quote: A concern arises when comparing activity between conditions for a certain stimulus: observed differences could arise and be confounded by block-to-block differences in baseline fluorescence. To account for this concern, we baseline corrected all time-courses on a trial level. Further, when calculating the condition contrasts, we performed a trial condition shuffle control. This first involved computing trial-averaged activity with trial conditions shuffled within each block (effectively preserving block-to-block differences in activity, while eliminating condition-dependent differences). The condition contrast was then computed (MMR or DD). Finally, trial-averaged shuffle data were subtracted from trial condition-intact data on a ROI-by-ROI basis.

span.label: THE CONTROL AREA IS SPOILED BY THE SELECTION PROCEDURE: the stimuli were chosen to drive parietal cortex, so a null in visual cortex says nothing, and the paper says so
span.quote: MMN was not found to be significant for either stimuli in the VC ERPs (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). Although the difference between standard and deviant responses for Stimulus A is trending (t(6) = 2.36, p = 0.056), these results are difficult to interpret since the oddball stimuli were chosen based on PPC preference.

span.label: AND THE POPULATION AVERAGE SHOWS NOTHING: multi-unit firing gave no difference across conditions, with the signal proposed to live in select cells invisible to a neuron-averaged rate
span.quote: Furthermore, we found no differences in spiking magnitude across oddball conditions (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). It is possible, at least for PPC, that the MMN is a specialized signal present in select cells and is not immediately apparent in the general neuron-averaged multi-unit firing rate.

span.label: the negative result is defended rather than buried: the absence of deviance detection is named as something that might be read as diminishing the study, and then turned into the contribution
span.quote: Further, it may be construed that the lack of deviance detection in our results diminishes the significance of our study; however, by demonstrating that stimulus-dependent adaptation manifests across sparsely encoded cells, our findings build upon several seminal works that highlight the contribution of adaptation to MMN 16 , 17 , 59 . Our novel contribution to this adaptation hypothesis is that this attenuation of the ERP obligatory component may depend on single neuron stimulus preference.

span.label: and an internal tension is stated outright - stimulus-specific mismatch responses but adaptation for both stimuli - with a proposed resolution offered as a proposal
span.quote: Finally, it is important to reconcile that we observed stimulus-specific MMR in the calcium imaging results, but SSA for both stimuli. We believe the stimulus-specific component of the MMR could arise from suppression of activity in the opponent stimulus’ deviant condition. Such a phenomenon could serve as a signal-to-noise amplification mechanism for stimulus presentation frequency differentiation in the local PPC circuitry.

span.label: THE STIMULUS CARRIES TWO FEATURES AT ONCE: opposing directions share an orientation, and orientation does not change between conditions, so the missing effect for one stimulus may be about which feature the cells are tracking
span.quote: Finally, it is possible to explain the stimulus-specific MMN results in the context of the multiplexing of stimulus direction and orientation. Stimuli with opposing directions share the same orientation and therefore with the stimuli chosen in our study, PPC neurons may contend with both orientation and direction information. This is particularly important for the opponent stimulus where PPC activity could be dominated more by the stimulus orientation rather than direction. Since orientation remains invariant across standard and deviant conditions, this may explain the lack of MMN for the opponent stimulus.

span.label: replicates → the monkey inferior temporal cortex visual oddball study (ref. 14), on MMN being explained by adaptation
span.quote: Here we find similar results where the MMN can be explained primarily by adaptation; however, our single-cell 2-photon calcium imaging analysis revealed putative neurons that showed more prominent MMN and adaptation for one stimulus over the other.

span.label: builds-on → seminal works on the contribution of adaptation to MMN (refs. 16, 17, 59)
span.quote: Further, it may be construed that the lack of deviance detection in our results diminishes the significance of our study; however, by demonstrating that stimulus-dependent adaptation manifests across sparsely encoded cells, our findings build upon several seminal works that highlight the contribution of adaptation to MMN 16 , 17 , 59 .

span.label: extends → existing models of MMN generation
span.quote: Together, our results provide an extension to existing models of MMN whereby patches of PPC neurons up- and down-regulate activity as a function of stimulus and condition.

span.label: replicates → reports of opposing-direction tuning in parietal cortex of other species (refs. 20, 22)
span.quote: We found that ferret posterior parietal cortex (PPC) firing activity and local field potentials (LFP) primarily showed strong responses to two opposing directions, similar to reports in other animal species (Fig. 1 B,D) 20 , 22 .

span.label: supports → the monkey inferotemporal oddball study that found no difference between deviant and many-standards control, so that the mismatch is explained by adaptation
span.quote: An important visual oddball study in monkey inferior temporal (IT) cortex revealed stronger responses in the deviant condition compared to the standard (MMN), but failed to find a difference between deviant and many-standard equiprobable control condition 14 . Here we find similar results where the MMN can be explained primarily by adaptation; however, our single-cell 2-photon calcium imaging analysis revealed putative neurons that showed more prominent MMN and adaptation for one stimulus over the other.

span.label: extends → the adaptation account of mismatch negativity, by adding that the attenuation may depend on single-neuron stimulus preference
span.quote: Further, it may be construed that the lack of deviance detection in our results diminishes the significance of our study; however, by demonstrating that stimulus-dependent adaptation manifests across sparsely encoded cells, our findings build upon several seminal works that highlight the contribution of adaptation to MMN 16 , 17 , 59 . Our novel contribution to this adaptation hypothesis is that this attenuation of the ERP obligatory component may depend on single neuron stimulus preference.

span.label: builds-on → the three-block oddball design that allows the same stimulus to be compared across conditions, described as becoming the new standard
span.quote: Importantly, this version of the oddball paradigm is rapidly becoming the new standard in the field since it allows for the comparison of neuronal responses across conditions for each stimulus

span.label: supports → work implicating somatostatin interneurons in mismatch modulation, whose inactivation impairs frequency differentiation
span.quote: Alternatively, recent work has provided support for the causal involvement of somatostatin-positive (SOM+) neurons in MMN modulation 54 . Inspired by reports of inhibitory interneuron involvement in lateral inhibition and regulation of surround suppression 56 , 57 , one mechanistic explanation could be that these SOM+ neurons facilitating SSA by inhibiting pyramidal neurons during the standard condition 36 . Indeed, evidence shows that the suppression of activity may arise from SOM+ interneurons regulation of pyramidal neurons, as reversible inactivation of SOM+ neurons impair differentiation of stimulus presentation frequency in population activity

span.label: supports → the schizophrenia account linking NMDA receptor and parvalbumin interneuron dysfunction to reduced gamma power
span.quote: Our results may provide insight to the mechanisms underlying the dysfunction of oddball-related sensory processing deficits in psychiatric disorders. One prominent mechanistic theory in schizophrenia research revolves around the role of N-methyl D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr)-dependent parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneuron activity 37 – 39 . Gamma oscillations arise from the interaction between excitatory pyramidal neurons and PV+ interneurons 40 – 42 . Further, NMDArs are causally involved in the regulation of PV+ neuron-mediated gamma oscillations 43 . As reduced gamma power has been associated with cognitive and sensory processing deficits in patients with schizophrenia 39 , 44 , it is hypothesized that NMDAr and PV+ interneuron dysfunction are underlying causes

span.label: GCaMP —renamed-across-fields→ MMR
span.quote: The comparison between standard and deviant conditions for the calcium imaging data was called mismatch response (MMR) due to the GCaMP protein exhibiting primarily positive increases in activity and its slow decay kinetics.

span.label: ROI —operationalised-as→ MMR
span.quote: Indeed, ROI-averaged responses showed consistently higher activity for the preferred stimulus in the deviant condition compared to the standard condition across the period of 300–1,500 ms relative to stimulus onset (Fig. 4 C,D, paired t test; t(72) = 3.71, p = 0.001; Holm-Bonferroni corrected). We did not find a significant difference between standard and deviant conditions for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(72) = 0.022, p = 0.982; Holm-Bonferroni corrected), further confirming that MMR occurs in parietal cortex in a stimulus-specific manner.

span.label: control —distinct-from→ standard
span.quote: A third block’s (many-standards control block) stimuli consisted of 10 equiprobable drifting gratings of different motion directions (same structure and stimuli as the initial tuning curve session); stimuli presented in this third condition served as controls that do not elicit adaptation effects of the standard condition or surprise effects like the deviant condition.

span.label: control —distinct-from→ deviant
span.quote: The three blocks allowed for comparing the responses to the same stimulus across the standard (frequent presentation: 90% of trials), deviant (rare presentation: 10% of trials), and control (rare, but without a history of a repeated stimulus: 10% of trials) contexts.

span.label: standard —contrasted-with→ deviant
span.quote: In one block (oddball A), the two best responsive stimuli from the first session were chosen to be presented in either the standard (90% of trials) or deviant (10% of trials) condition (ie. stimulus A was the deviant and B was the standard). In another block (oddball B), the same two stimuli were used but the conditions were switched (ie. stimulus B was the deviant and A was the standard). The reason for presenting both of these blocks is to be able to compare the same stimulus presented in different conditions, thus removing the confounding factor of stimulus-preference when examining neural activity.

span.label: MMR —part-of→ DD
span.quote: The MMR can be dissected into two key components characterizing the surprise (deviance detection—DD) and adaptation (stimulus-specific adaptation—SSA) responses by comparing the control condition to the deviant or standard condition, respectively. To investigate the distribution of condition-dependent responses across ROIs, we reanalyzed the data by computing condition contrasts (ie. MMR, DD, and SSA) as a function of stimuli for each ROI

span.label: MMR —part-of→ SSA
span.quote: The MMR can be dissected into two key components characterizing the surprise (deviance detection—DD) and adaptation (stimulus-specific adaptation—SSA) responses by comparing the control condition to the deviant or standard condition, respectively. To investigate the distribution of condition-dependent responses across ROIs, we reanalyzed the data by computing condition contrasts (ie. MMR, DD, and SSA) as a function of stimuli for each ROI

span.label: SSA —distinct-from→ opponent
span.quote: In the distribution of time-averaged SSA across ROIs, both stimuli showed a similar amount of adaptation (Fig. 4 H; preferred stimulus: μ = 2.067, σ = 1.490; opponent stimulus: μ = 1.555, σ = 1.018; stimulus contrast: μ = -0.512, σ = 1.616; paired t test; t (72) = 0.659, p = 0.512; Holm-Bonferroni corrected).

span.label: DD —distinct-from→ preferred
span.quote: There was an absence of DD (deviant vs. control) for the preferred stimulus (paired t test; t (72) = 1.39, p = 0.168; Holm-Bonferroni corrected). Although not statistically significant, the deviant condition responses for the opponent stimulus were lower in magnitude than the control condition (paired t test; t (72) = 2.07, p = 0.085, Holm-Bonferroni corrected). In the time-averaged distribution, a negative DD indicated lower deviant activity compared to control (Fig. 4 G 3rd column; μ = − 1.352, σ = 1.304). DD magnitude was significantly different between the two stimuli in the stimulus contrast

span.label: MMR —causes→ preferred
span.quote: Indeed, ROI-averaged responses showed consistently higher activity for the preferred stimulus in the deviant condition compared to the standard condition across the period of 300–1,500 ms relative to stimulus onset (Fig. 4 C,D, paired t test; t(72) = 3.71, p = 0.001; Holm-Bonferroni corrected). We did not find a significant difference between standard and deviant conditions for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(72) = 0.022, p = 0.982; Holm-Bonferroni corrected), further confirming that MMR occurs in parietal cortex in a stimulus-specific manner.

span.label: MMN —operationalised-as→ gamma
span.quote: When we analyzed the 150–250 ms MMN epoch, we found a significant difference in the 25–50 Hz gamma frequency band power between the preferred stimulus standard and deviant conditions, where the deviant condition exhibited higher power (Fig. 2 B,C, paired t test; t(14) = 2.25, p = 0.041), but not for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(14) = 0.860, p = 0.404).

span.label: gamma —contrasted-with→ alpha
span.quote: To examine if oddball condition differentiation was specific to the gamma frequency band or a general feature across multiple frequency bands, we calculated alpha frequency band power as a function of condition and stimulus. Condition differentiation was not observed in the alpha frequency band for either stimuli (Fig. 2 D,E, preferred stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 0.958, p = 0.354; opponent stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 0.404, p = 0.692), indicating again stimulus-specific MMN that was selectively reflected in both the raw ERP and specifically in the gamma frequency band.

span.label: MMN —operationalised-as→ preferred
span.quote: We found a significantly larger magnitude negative deflection in the event-related potential (150–250 ms MMN epoch, Fig. 1 G) for the population-preferred stimulus presented in the deviant conditions compared to that of in the standard conditions (Fig. 1 H, preferred stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 2.16, p = 0.048). Such conditions differentiation was not found for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(14) = 0.252, p = 0.805).

span.label: MMN —operationalised-as→ ERP
span.quote: To examine if oddball condition differentiation was specific to the gamma frequency band or a general feature across multiple frequency bands, we calculated alpha frequency band power as a function of condition and stimulus. Condition differentiation was not observed in the alpha frequency band for either stimuli (Fig. 2 D,E, preferred stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 0.958, p = 0.354; opponent stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 0.404, p = 0.692), indicating again stimulus-specific MMN that was selectively reflected in both the raw ERP and specifically in the gamma frequency band.

span.label: spiking —distinct-from→ MMN
span.quote: Furthermore, we found no differences in spiking magnitude across oddball conditions (Supplementary Fig. 4 ). It is possible, at least for PPC, that the MMN is a specialized signal present in select cells and is not immediately apparent in the general neuron-averaged multi-unit firing rate.

span.label: VC —distinct-from→ PPC
span.quote: MMN was not found to be significant for either stimuli in the VC ERPs (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). Although the difference between standard and deviant responses for Stimulus A is trending (t(6) = 2.36, p = 0.056), these results are difficult to interpret since the oddball stimuli were chosen based on PPC preference.

span.label: shuffle —operationalised-as→ ROI
span.quote: A concern arises when comparing activity between conditions for a certain stimulus: observed differences could arise and be confounded by block-to-block differences in baseline fluorescence. To account for this concern, we baseline corrected all time-courses on a trial level. Further, when calculating the condition contrasts, we performed a trial condition shuffle control. This first involved computing trial-averaged activity with trial conditions shuffled within each block (effectively preserving block-to-block differences in activity, while eliminating condition-dependent differences). The condition contrast was then computed (MMR or DD). Finally, trial-averaged shuffle data were subtracted from trial condition-intact data on a ROI-by-ROI basis.

span.label: modulation index —operationalised-as→ MMR
span.quote: To quantify an ROI’s stimulus preference, a modulation index was calculated: S pref - S Opp S pref + S Opp where S Pref and S Opp corresponded to the trial-averaged response during the 300–1,500 ms epoch to the preferred stimulus and opponent stimulus, respectively. span.label: tuning —operationalised-as→ preferred

span.label: MMR
span.quote: Indeed, ROI-averaged responses showed consistently higher activity for the preferred stimulus in the deviant condition compared to the standard condition across the period of 300–1,500 ms relative to stimulus onset (Fig. 4 C,D, paired t test; t(72) = 3.71, p = 0.001; Holm-Bonferroni corrected). We did not find a significant difference between standard and deviant conditions for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(72) = 0.022, p = 0.982; Holm-Bonferroni corrected), further confirming that MMR occurs in parietal cortex in a stimulus-specific manner.

In the time-averaged distribution, a negative DD indicated lower deviant activity compared to control (Fig. 4 G 3rd column; μ = − 1.352, σ = 1.304). span.label: gamma
span.quote: When we analyzed the 150–250 ms MMN epoch, we found a significant difference in the 25–50 Hz gamma frequency band power between the preferred stimulus standard and deviant conditions, where the deviant condition exhibited higher power (Fig. 2 B,C, paired t test; t(14) = 2.25, p = 0.041), but not for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(14) = 0.860, p = 0.404).

span.label: tuning
span.quote: We found that ferret posterior parietal cortex (PPC) firing activity and local field potentials (LFP) primarily showed strong responses to two opposing directions, similar to reports in other animal species (Fig. 1 B,D) 20 , 22 . The stimulus direction that elicited the largest normalized amplitude was deemed the preferred stimulus and the stimulus drifting in the opposite direction, which typically showed the second largest response, was deemed the opponent stimulus.

span.quote: Three animals were included in the electrophysiological experiment (across these animals, we acquired 15 sessions) and four were included in the 2-photon calcium imaging experiment (across these animals, we acquired 21 sessions).

span.quote: the majority of ROIs showed congruent stimulus preference to the population (MI values greater than 0) and a minority preferred the opponent stimulus (MI values less than 0)

span.label: 150 — the start of the mismatch window in milliseconds, a boundary imported whole from the human literature
span.quote: Specifically, the mismatch negativity (MMN) is a neurophysiological difference waveform peaking in the 150–250 ms window after stimulus onset. The MMN refers to the difference in evoked response to the standard and deviant stimulus. Importantly, the MMN is distinct from the N100 (occurring between 50 and 150 ms post stimulus onset) and the P300 (occurring around 300–400 ms) components with respect to function and timing relative to stimulus onset

span.label: 90% — share of trials in the standard, with the deviant and the control at 10% each, across the three contexts
span.quote: The three blocks allowed for comparing the responses to the same stimulus across the standard (frequent presentation: 90% of trials), deviant (rare presentation: 10% of trials), and control (rare, but without a history of a repeated stimulus: 10% of trials) contexts.

span.label: n = 73 — regions passing the response criterion, a low yield attributed to parietal activity being task driven
span.quote: ROIs that exhibited stimulus-evoked activity (300–1,500 ms) 1.5 standard deviations above baseline (− 200 to 0 ms) mean activity for at least 400 consecutive milliseconds for at least 25% of trials, and 1.5 standard deviations above baseline mean activity for at least 400 consecutive milliseconds in the trial average were identified as visually responsive and were included for further analysis (n = 73).

span.label: 300 to 1,500 ms — the calcium analysis window, chosen because that is when the indicator has decayed rather than when the process occurs
span.quote: Due to the slow decay kinetics of the GCaMP6f fluorescence indicator, it is difficult to interpret when certain processes are occurring during periods of neural activity. Accordingly, we chose the period of time that calcium responses largely decayed back to baseline (from 300 to 1,500 ms relative to stimulus onset) when performing statistics or averaging across the epoch of time related to stimulus response.

span.label: t(14) = 2.16, p = 0.048 — the electrophysiological mismatch for the preferred stimulus, against t = 0.252 for the opponent
span.quote: We found a significantly larger magnitude negative deflection in the event-related potential (150–250 ms MMN epoch, Fig. 1 G) for the population-preferred stimulus presented in the deviant conditions compared to that of in the standard conditions (Fig. 1 H, preferred stimulus: paired t test; t(14) = 2.16, p = 0.048). Such conditions differentiation was not found for the opponent stimulus (paired t test; t(14) = 0.252, p = 0.805).

span.label: six adult — ferrets in total, three for electrophysiology and four for imaging, with one animal in neither role
span.quote: A total of six adult (16–19 weeks old) female ferrets ( Mustela putorius furo , weighing 0.7–1 kg, group housed in a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle; spayed, Marshall BioResources, North Rose, NY) were included in this study. Three animals were included in the electrophysiological experiment (across these animals, we acquired 15 sessions) and four were included in the 2-photon calcium imaging experiment (across these animals, we acquired 21 sessions).
